Detect regex matches, in parallel

Source: R/par-detect.R
par_detect.Rd

  • par_detect() is like grepl(pattern, x).

  • par_count() counts the matches in each string, as many as gregexpr() would find, but without building them.

Both run on several threads. They use the syntax of Rust's regex crate instead of R's. Most patterns mean the same in both. See Details for the differences.

Usage

par_detect(
  x,
  pattern,
  fixed = FALSE,
  nthreads = getOption("parvenu.threads", 0L)
)

par_count(
  x,
  pattern,
  fixed = FALSE,
  nthreads = getOption("parvenu.threads", 0L)
)

Arguments

x

A string vector, or an object convertible by as.character().

pattern

The regex, or the literal string to find if fixed = TRUE: one string, or one per string of x, as in stringi::stri_detect_regex(). Each distinct pattern is compiled once.

fixed

If TRUE, pattern is found as it is, as in grepl(fixed = TRUE): no character has a special meaning.

nthreads

A whole number: the max number of threads to use. 0 means the RAYON_NUM_THREADS environment variable, or else all cores. The default is the parvenu.threads option, or 0 if that isn't set. Inputs too small to keep that many threads busy get fewer, and more threads than cores count as all cores.

Value

A vector as long as x, NA where x or pattern is NA:

  • par_detect(): logical, TRUE where pattern matches and FALSE where it doesn't.

  • par_count(): integer, the number of non-overlapping matches.

Details

The syntax differs from R's in these ways:

  • No backreferences (\\1) or lookaround ((?=...)). In return, time grows only linearly with the length of the string. Engines that backtrack, such as PCRE (grepl(perl = TRUE)), try every way a pattern can split the string. That can take exponentially long: ^(a+)+$ against 25 as and a ! exceeds PCRE's match limit.

  • Unicode by default: \\d, \\w, and \\s match any Unicode digit, word, or space character. Write [0-9] or (?-u:\\d) for ASCII only.

  • Flags go in the pattern: (?i) ignores case.

  • NA returns NA, where grepl() returns FALSE.

The counts of par_count() differ from gregexpr() only for patterns that can match the empty string, such as "", "a*", or "\\b". The two engines treat empty matches in opposite ways:

  • At the end of a string, par_count() counts an empty match and gregexpr() doesn't (unless the string itself is empty). So "" has 4 matches in "abc", where gregexpr() finds 3.

  • Right after a non-empty match, gregexpr() counts an empty match and par_count() doesn't. So "a*" has 4 matches in "banana": an empty one before the "b", and the three "a"s. gregexpr() also finds an empty one after each of the first two "a"s, so 6.

The threads read the strings straight from R's memory, as data.table does.

Examples

par_detect(c("apple", "banana", NA), "an+a", nthreads = 2)
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE    NA
par_detect("ABC", "(?i)b")
#> [1] TRUE
par_detect(c("a.c", "abc"), ".", fixed = TRUE)
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE
par_detect(c("apple", "banana", "cherry"), c("^a", "an", "z")) # one each
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE
par_count(c("banana", "kiwi", NA), "an")
#> [1]  2  0 NA
